content.p: On the morning of Wednesday 30 September 2026, a Flydubai Boeing 737 MAX 8 on its way from Dubai to Tel Aviv fell more than 17,000 feet in about two minutes while its two pilots fought on the cockpit floor. The captain, an Indian national named Smit Machchhar, had been attacked by his own co-pilot. Badly wounded, he managed to unlock the cockpit door. Passengers and crew rushed in, dragged the co-pilot out and tied him up, and other pilots travelling on the flight landed the aircraft at Tabuk in northwestern Saudi Arabia. No passenger was seriously hurt.

Three days later the attorney general of the United Arab Emirates said the co-pilot had used the cockpit's crash axe and had tried to take over the aircraft in what he called an attempted terrorist act. Investigators said they were still working to establish his motive and whether anyone else was involved.

Flight FZ1073 left Dubai at 7:05 a.m. and climbed to 34,000 feet, according to the tracking service Flightradar24. Most of the people on board were Israelis heading home. Tzvika Manes, a banking executive, told CNN that he and his family were returning from a holiday in Tokyo with a layover in Dubai. Four passengers also held American citizenship, two US officials said.

Accounts of how many people were on the aircraft differ. Israel's Foreign Ministry and Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu spoke of 174 lives saved. Flydubai's chief executive, Ghaith Al Ghaith, referred to 172 passengers and crew. The Associated Press put the figure at 182. The Israeli news site Ynetnews reported that 27 children were among the passengers.

In command was Machchhar, a 39-year-old father of two who comes from Mumbai and lives in Dubai. He had been flying for 17 years, 11 of them as a captain. The first officer beside him had worked for Flydubai for only eight months, an Israeli official told CNN.

A little more than two hours after take-off, with Tel Aviv about an hour away, the co-pilot attacked the captain inside the locked cockpit. Passengers and Israeli officials at first described a stabbing. On Saturday 3 October the UAE attorney general, Hamad Saif Al Shamsi, said the weapon was the crash axe, a tool that airliners carry so a crew can break through a window or a panel in an emergency.

Machchhar described what happened in a video call with India's prime minister, Narendra Modi, that Modi's office released. Speaking in Hindi from a hospital in Abu Dhabi, he said he was on the floor and being beaten when he felt the aircraft plunging. "This is the last push, Smit, do it, the door is right there," he recalled telling himself. "Somehow, I opened the door, and everyone came in," he said.

While the two men struggled, the aircraft was out of control. Flight-tracking data showed it falling about 17,400 feet in less than two minutes, then climbing, then falling again. Flightradar24 recorded vertical speeds ranging from about 30,000 feet per minute downward to 10,000 feet per minute upward, and said the figure rarely passes 4,000 in normal flying. Passenger Adam Polo told CNN that the power, the entertainment system and the air conditioning cut out and that anyone standing in the aisle fell. The Associated Press reported that the descent was violent enough to tear away part of the rudder.

Manes said his wife had taken their six-year-old daughter to the toilet when she heard shouting and fighting from the cockpit. She woke one of the additional pilots travelling on the flight, then saw the cockpit door open and the captain under attack.

Yaniv Hayoun, an Israeli plumber, later described to Netanyahu how he got into the cockpit. The wounded captain was up against the door, he said, which made it hard to open at first. Neither pilot was in his seat, he said, and the co-pilot seemed to be trying to disable the aircraft. Hayoun said he put the man in a chokehold, dragged him out, then went back and pulled on the controls until a pilot took over. He said he knew what to do from watching a television programme that reconstructs air disasters.

Shota Musaev, a dentist, told CNN he ran forward and found the attacker on top of the captain. The co-pilot was bound with headphone cords and plastic zip ties, and Musaev treated Machchhar, who he said had suffered "massive blood loss". Musaev told ABC News that the restrained man said he was from Oman and at one point asked to be killed. Another passenger, Assaf Rajuan, said about five others helped him subdue the attacker. Fear lingered afterwards, he said, because nobody knew whom to trust. "We even started suspecting the flight attendants," he told CNN.

Flydubai said the aircraft was secured by on-duty crew travelling on the flight, who diverted it and landed it. A passenger described them as two relief pilots who had been due to operate a later flight. They have not been publicly identified.

The aircraft levelled out at about 15,000 feet. Its transponder showed 7700, the general emergency code, and then 7500, the code for unlawful interference. An Israeli official told CBS News that the Israeli Air Force had already noticed the flight leaving its path and losing height. When it could not reach the crew, it closed Israeli airspace and scrambled jets, although the aircraft was still several hundred miles away. The jets stayed inside Israeli airspace once it was clear that the flight had turned toward Saudi Arabia, which had scrambled jets of its own. The official said the whole episode lasted about 15 minutes.

The operator of Tabuk's airport, Cluster2 Airports, said the request for an emergency landing came at 8:44 a.m. and that the aircraft landed at 9:45 a.m. local time. Both pilots were taken to hospital. In a video posted from the aircraft, Rajuan appealed for help and said all the passengers were fine, but not the pilot.

Saudi Arabia rejected an Israeli request to send an aircraft for the passengers, CNN reported. Flydubai sent two replacement aircraft to Tabuk, and the passengers reached Ben Gurion Airport that evening, where relatives were waiting and people sang as they came off the flight.

UAE authorities have not named the co-pilot. The Associated Press, citing three people with knowledge of the situation, among them a Gulf diplomat and a Western diplomat, identified him as Hamam al-Hammami, an Omani national. CNN reported the same name from two sources and an Israeli official, and ABC News gave his age as 29. CBS News spelled the name al Hamami. Oman's government has not publicly confirmed his nationality.

What is known of his past comes largely from unnamed officials. They say he was born in the UAE to an Omani father and a Syrian mother and spent much of his life outside Oman. A LinkedIn profile in his name, which one source told CNN was his, listed seven years at Oman Air ending in February 2025. Officials told ABC News that in 2024, while he was a co-pilot trainee there, he was found with extremist materials and was moved to an administrative role. Sources told CBS News that Omani government surveillance had found him visiting radical websites and that he resigned after being put on desk duty. Royal Air Maroc told the Associated Press that he completed three months of theoretical training with it in 2025 and was not selected for a job. Buckinghamshire New University in England said he had completed a distance-learning course in aviation management and had taken no pilot training there.

The Gulf diplomat told the Associated Press that the co-pilot went through standard security checks before Flydubai hired him, but that those checks appeared to look for criminal convictions and not for signs of radicalisation. Sources told CBS News that the airline did not vet him with the Omani government.

CNN reported that two posts appeared on the LinkedIn profile about nine hours after the attack. One was a video of cockpit footage and of Israeli airliners at Dubai's airport, ending with photographs of the al Qaeda leader Ayman al-Zawahiri and of the man who carried out a 2009 suicide bombing that killed CIA officers. It is not known who published the posts or whether they had been scheduled in advance. The profile was later deleted, as was an Instagram account in the same name.

Saudi Arabia's Interior Ministry said on Thursday 1 October that a preliminary inquiry, carried out with a UAE security team, had found "an assault on the captain by the co-pilot, resulting in various injuries to both". Both men left for Abu Dhabi that morning with an Emirati security team. The UAE said its courts have jurisdiction because the aircraft is registered there, and because its law applies to crimes on board its aircraft even outside the country.

On 3 October Al Shamsi said the co-pilot "began executing his plan during the flight, attacking the captain inside the flight deck using a crash axe and attempting to take control of the aircraft". He said work was continuing on the motive, on any links to other people and on the physical and digital evidence, and that the final results would be announced.

Israeli leaders spoke sooner and more sharply. On the day of the attack Israel's defence minister, Israel Katz, called it "an attempted jihadist terror attack". Netanyahu said Israel knew that the co-pilot "underwent Islamist radical indoctrination", though he gave no evidence, and later said Israel was investigating whether the man had been sent by someone. He said the UAE's president had agreed that Israel would join the questioning. President Donald Trump said the co-pilot might be linked to Iran, without giving details, while Netanyahu said it was too early to say. The Gulf diplomat told the Associated Press that the inquiry had found no connection with militant groups so far. Sources briefed on the investigation told ABC News that the co-pilot was cooperating and had indicated that he intended to crash the aircraft in Israel.

The attack exposed a gap that neither country has explained. Oman has no formal diplomatic relations with Israel, and Israel says its agreements with foreign carriers keep pilots from such countries off flights to its airports. Transportation Minister Miri Regev made the same argument about the aviation agreement with the UAE. Israeli agencies including Shin Bet and Mossad began examining how the co-pilot came to be part of the crew. The attack fell a week before the anniversary of the Hamas-led attack of 7 October 2023, and weeks before an Israeli election in which security failures were already a central issue.

Israel suspended Flydubai flights to Ben Gurion for six days, Ynetnews reported, and the airline suspended its Tel Aviv operations until further notice at the request of the authorities. Al Ghaith said a full official investigation was under way and that it should be allowed to establish the facts.

Machchhar was treated first in Tabuk and then in Abu Dhabi, where India's embassy said he was recovering well. Modi called him a hero, Netanyahu said he had prevented "a 9/11 disaster", and the artist Sudarsan Pattnaik made a sand sculpture in his honour on Puri beach. In his call with Modi, Machchhar said everyone who came through the door had an equal role in the rescue. "I was trying to save myself," he said, "but I also knew that I can't let anyone die."
